title: The Monarch's Role in Constitutional Safeguards
label: 16 September 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: The Constitution Committee heard from Lord Young of Old Windsor, former principal private secretary to the sovereign, about the monarch's constitutional role, the importance of confidentiality in the weekly audience with the Prime Minister, and how reserve powers might operate in extreme scenarios. Lord Young argued that the system works well in practice due to trust and good faith, but acknowledged risks if those conventions break down.

speakers.label: Lord Young of Old Windsor
speakers.name: Lord Young of Old Windsor
speakers.role: Former principal private secretary to the sovereign

chapters.title: The Weekly Audience
chapters.takeaway: The private weekly meeting between the monarch and the Prime Minister is central to the constitutional relationship, allowing confidential advice and warning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Young, how would you describe the monarch's constitutional role in day-to-day governance?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I was in the room for six or seven Prime Ministerial appointments. The core is the weekly audience with the PM, usually on Wednesdays after PMQs. It's a private hour where the sovereign can be consulted, encourage and warn. The PM always seemed to walk in a bit taller afterwards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the privacy of that meeting is crucial.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Absolutely. That confidentiality is the crux. Without it, you can't have the candid conversations that make the system work. It's like the protection of policy formulation under the Freedom of Information Act—you need space to talk freely.

chapters.title: Reserve Powers and Their Limits
chapters.takeaway: The monarch has reserve powers that could theoretically be used in extreme situations, but they are rarely needed because the system relies on good faith and trust.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Beyond that weekly hour, could the monarch act as a constitutional restraint on a Government?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, in theory. For example, if it's unclear who should be Prime Minister, or if a PM losing a confidence vote asks for a Prorogation or dissolution. The sovereign might decline. But if things are working well, it should never come to that. The perception of power is often enough—the fear that the sovereign might say no.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: What if a PM loses a no-confidence vote but refuses to resign, there's no alternative figure, and deadlock? What happens then?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It would depend on the personalities and political mood. The sovereign might exercise greater power, even dismissal, but that's a last resort. In practice, a PM who lost their Cabinet and couldn't pass legislation wouldn't last long anyway.

chapters.title: A Real Constitutional Test: Boris Johnson and Covid
chapters.takeaway: During Boris Johnson's hospitalisation with Covid, a potential constitutional crisis was averted through cooperation and planning, showing the system's flexibility.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: Is it beneficial that the sovereign's residual powers are somewhat opaque, allowing them to develop in novel situations?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. Take the time Boris Johnson was hospitalised with Covid and feared to be near death. There was no Deputy PM. We had to work out what to advise the Queen. The plan was for the Cabinet Secretary to summon the Cabinet and force them to choose a temporary PM, with cross-party support. It never happened, but it showed how people coming together can handle a crisis.

chapters.title: Transparency, Trust, and the Monarchy
chapters.takeaway: The monarchy builds trust through long-term, non-partisan actions, balancing the need for confidentiality with public visibility.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: How do you encourage public trust when so much depends on discretion and confidentiality?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It's a paradox. But the monarchy thinks in decades, not election cycles. By convening groups, recognising service, and representing the nation consistently, it builds trust over time. That's something a politician can't do.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: So it's about visibility?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, through the head of nation role.

chapters.title: The King's Neutrality and Constitutional Guardians
chapters.takeaway: The King has successfully transitioned from advocating causes as Prince of Wales to a neutral monarch, and the private secretary acts as a constitutional guardian.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: The King was outspoken on issues like climate change as Prince of Wales. How does he manage neutrality now?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It's accepted that as heir you can pursue interests, but once you take the top job, you set them aside. He made that clear, and the transition has been smooth. Fears of an interventionist King haven't materialised.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Is the private secretary to the monarch a guardian of the constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, among others. The principles have been consistent for decades.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Sir Alan Lascelles wrote a letter to The Times in 1950 clarifying constitutional principles. Is that part of the role?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, trying to anticipate constitutional difficulties is key. Though today, an anonymous letter might not work—you need subtler methods.

chapters.title: Safeguards in a Determined Government
chapters.takeaway: If a democratically elected Government with a majority pursues radical policies, there are few constitutional safeguards to stop it; the system relies on conventions and good faith.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: If an elected Government introduced censorship, could the monarchy act as a backstop?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If it were a manifesto commitment and passed into law, it would be very difficult for a sovereign or the courts to overturn. That's the nature of parliamentary democracy.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: So in the face of a determined Government controlling Parliament, are there any safeguards that could withstand them?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If they have a majority and a manifesto mandate, it's hard to argue it's constitutionally improper. The system relies on conventions and good faith, which have held so far, but we shouldn't be complacent.
